description: In 2004 PayPal restricted Nigerian users from receiving funds entirely, citing fraud. A 2014 partnership with First Bank of Nigeria was send-only and heavily restricted. PayPal returned in January 2026 via a partnership with Paga, allowing users to receive from 200+ countries and withdraw in naira.
energy_note: Twenty-two years of being able to pay and not be paid.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the $9,000 that did not arrive
description: One remote worker recalled losing access to a $9,000 payment in 2023 after PayPal refused to remit funds without clear reasons. Many Nigerian freelancers lost contracts outright because clients preferred PayPal and would not use anything else.
energy_note: Nine thousand dollars, earned, and simply not released.

aspect: The stated reason, and the comparison that undermines it
description: PayPal cited high fraud rates, compliance risk, weak national identification and banking regulation. Meanwhile Nigerian fintechs such as Flutterwave and Paystack built functioning payment systems without mass account lockouts - and PayPal's 2026 return is built on the infrastructure those companies created.
energy_note: Too risky to serve, and now returning on rails Nigerians built.

aspect: The model was selective exclusion, not absence
description: One characterisation: users could send but not receive, and were flagged, frozen or limited disproportionately under vague risk policies. That is worse than a clean absence, because it lets a person build a business on a rail that will drop them.
energy_note: Allowed to pay them. Not allowed to be paid.

aspect: The return does not repair the twenty years
description: Critics note the partnership does not fix the underlying problems, and that the businesses that failed for want of a payment method between 2004 and 2026 are not recoverable.
energy_note: Two decades of companies that could not take money.
